text.default:
They lead you through the outskirts as easily as somebody who has done it hundreds of times, and very likely they have. They know which stones to step round, which ways are thick with the curse, and which parts are safer. They have had fourteen months of learning the place the hard way.

The inner approach begins at a particular spot. What looks from outside like a fallen wall turns out, from the right angle, to be the mouth of a passage going down. The floor slopes gently and the walls close in. The stone here is older than the stone above, darker and smoother, worn by centuries of hands.

Here the carvings begin.

They cover everything, the walls and the ceiling and even parts of the floor. They are close and careful and leave no space anywhere, as though whoever made them was racing against time and needed every inch. You cannot read a word. [missing person] can read some of it, though not all, as one reads a language learned late in life, slowly and approximately and without the idioms.
text.commander:
You walk the approach as you would any strange position, looking for cover, and for places to see from, and where you would want to be if something came at you from either end.

It is a corridor, and corridors are bad places. But the carvings make the walls uneven, and that would hinder any large body of men trying to come through. Whoever built this did not expect to defend it with soldiers. They expected to defend it with what they knew.
text.arcane:
The carvings keep drawing your eye even while you walk. You find yourself reading them as one reads things one is not meant to be reading, catching bits and pieces, putting together half a translation, and trying to keep all of it in your head at once.

The language is old, older than any tradition you know. But it has something in common with several dead languages you have studied, and from that you can work out, not words, but rules: how a sentence is put together, and how it says that one thing caused another.

You will have to come back here when you have time.
text.ranger:
You walk the approach with your hand kept off the wall, for you learned in the passage up above that this stone is not to be trusted, and you look the place over as you would a burrow or a den.

Something lived in this passage once. The signs are old, from before the ruins were left empty. The floor is worn in a way that means people came along here every day for centuries. This was not a way in for ceremonies. It was a corridor people used.
text.cipher:
You walk along and watch how [missing person] goes through the approach. They are showing you the way they know, and so also the way they chose to learn. In every turning they take and every wall they avoid you can read their fourteen months.

They are not afraid here. That is the most important thing you notice. They came into this place fourteen months ago and learned it and are not afraid of it. Either that is a remarkable piece of adapting, or it is something you ought to be a good deal more worried about than you are.

success.text:
They stop and look at one stretch of wall. "This part," they say, pointing, "is the history. What the city was for. The power they were holding, where it came from, and why they built the mechanism to hold it."

They go a little further. "This part tells you how to keep the mechanism in order. How often it needed seeing to, and what happened if it was neglected."

They stop again. "And this part is what I spent eight months on. The sealing ritual, the whole text, with every precaution and every requirement and every risk. The builders were honest about the risks." They look at you. "I will show you what matters when we reach the chamber."

success_at_cost.text: They give you the main divisions of it, the history, the upkeep, the ritual, and show you where the ritual begins. The details are beyond you for now, but it helps to know how it is laid out.

failure.text: They explain, but the explanation doesn't quite reach you. The ideas are too far from anything you know, and the words arrive without the sense. You keep what you can, and go on.

choices.text: "What was the first month like? Before you understood any of it?"

default.text:
They walk a little way before they answer.

"Terrifying," they say. "And then not. The first month I kept expecting to die, or to lose myself as the afflicted do. I kept trying things out, a little at a time, and drawing back, and learning where the worst of it was." They pause. "Some time in the second month I stopped being afraid and began to be curious. I have thought about that a great deal since. Whether the curiosity was mine, or the ruins'."

"And what did you decide?"

"That it may not matter as much as I used to think," they say. "The curiosity is real, and I am following it. Where it came from..." They glance at you. "I should like to know that, when this is over."

text.default:
The mark on the cellar wall turns out to be a crack between two leaning walls, behind a fall of stone that looks like nothing at all until you are standing on it.

[missing person] goes first, sideways. The crack goes down in steps that are not quite steps. Nobody has carved any writing in here. The walls are bare, and the air is cleaner than in the outskirts.

At the height of your hand, all the way down, somebody has scratched little figures into the stone. There are dozens of them, each the size of your thumb, and all the same shape as the one from Harrow. Some have marks beside them: a line, or two lines, or a ring.

"Tally marks," [missing person] says. "He was counting something."

default.text:
There are forty-one. You count them twice. The last has no marks beside it at all, and below it, in letters so small you need the lamp to read them, there is a name: JOREN.

[missing person] reads it over your shoulder and says nothing. They wait until you are ready to go on.

choices.text: Keep going. The chamber is below.

default.text: You go on down. The figures go with you, one every few steps, until the crack opens out above the chamber entrance, and there they stop.

text.default:
They stop in the passage some way short of the chamber. You can see the entrance ahead of you, a wider opening with a faint light coming out of it.

"Before we go in," they say, "there are some things you need to know."

They tell you.

The curse is thicker in the chamber than anywhere in Ashenveld. If you stay in there long without preparing yourself, you will suffer for it. The herbs from Maret's camp will help, and so will the Covenant's ward, but neither will protect you entirely.

The mechanism in the middle of the chamber gives off the curse, and it gives off something else as well, the power the city was built to hold. You must not touch the mechanism. They have been within three yards of it once, and it took three days to wear off.

"The ritual does not need you to touch it," they say. "Only to be near it. It is not the same thing."
text.commander:
"How do we get out if it goes wrong?" you ask.

"The way we came," they say. "The passage holds, and you can get through the outskirts. I have always been able to get out." They pause. "I was not expecting company when I planned my escape. I shall have to think again."

It takes you a moment to realise that this is a joke. It is the first they have made since you found them, and you feel something ease in your chest.
text.arcane:
"What happens to someone who's had too much of it?" you ask.

They tell you. First there is the narrowing, which you know already. Then time goes wrong; it runs unevenly, usually slower. Then there is what they call the hearing, though it is not really hearing, a feeling of the chamber's old purpose pressing in on you, as if you stood next to something very loud in a perfectly silent room. And last of all, in the worst cases, you can no longer tell where you end and everything else begins.

"Can you come back from the last one?" you ask.

"I think not," they say. "I have not tried it."
text.ranger:
"How will I know if I'm going too deep?" you ask. You mean too deep into the curse, not into the chamber.

They think about it. "When things stop mattering in the order they should," they say. "You will notice. The things that matter least go first." They pause. "For me, the first time, it was the cold. I stopped minding that I was cold. I noticed that before anything else, and I came out."

So that is your signal. When you stop minding the cold, you leave.
text.cipher:
"Who else knows how to get to this chamber?" you ask.

"Maret knows the outskirts," they say. "She does not know the inner approach. The Covenant has part of a map. I found signs they were here twenty years ago. But their map is old, and the outskirts have shifted since. The Compact has nothing."

They pause. "That may change, if Seriva is back."

"It will change," you say. "If she broke the seal, she knows exactly what she's looking for and how to find it."

text: You take what protection you have.

text.text: There are Maret's herbs, bitter under your tongue.
There is Edric's ward, cold against your skin.
You have nothing but what [missing person] has told you.

text: You know what to watch for now. You go in.

The light in the chamber is wrong. It is not the grey light of the outskirts. It is older than that, and seems to come out of the stone itself rather than from anywhere you can see. It is enough to see by, and somehow rather more than enough.

choices.text: Take time to prepare, and use what protection you have.

text.text: There are Maret's herbs, bitter under your tongue.
There is Edric's ward, cold against your skin.
You have nothing but what [missing person] has told you.

text: You and [missing person] go over how the chamber is laid out, what the ritual needs, and where they will want you to stand.
Getting ready does not take the danger away. It only changes what might go wrong.

text.default:
The chamber is large, and most of it is still standing.

In one corner the roof has come down, but there is no sky to be seen through the gap, only more stone, the higher levels of the buried city. The walls are carved from the floor up to the broken part, in the same close writing as the passage, but here there are drawings as well, plans and diagrams, as though an engineer had been at work on something that was not quite engineering.

In the middle of it stands the mechanism.

It is about three yards across, made of something fused together that is neither quite stone nor quite metal, and it is broken. You can see the break. It is a great split right through the main part of it, and it was not done by age or weather. Something struck it, and struck it on purpose.

Out of the break, just visible in the light of the chamber, rises a thread of something. It is not smoke, and not light either. It is like nothing you have ever seen. It rises from the crack and spreads into the air of the chamber, and from there, you understand now, it goes out through every seam of rock that joins this place to the world.
text.commander:
You look the mechanism over as you would a damaged wall. The break was meant. The angle of it, and the way the damage spreads, both point to one careful, deliberate blow, not to any accident or failing in the structure.

Somebody broke this on purpose. They did it carefully, and they knew what they were doing, and they did it all the same.

You look at the mechanism and think of Seriva.
text.arcane:
You stand at the safe distance [missing person] showed you, and read the walls of the chamber with everything you have.

The mechanism is a binding of the highest order. It is neither a cage nor a box. It is a change. The builders did not shut the power away; they gave it a shape. The shape was the city itself, its life, the never-ending business of tending the mechanism and keeping its rites and simply being there. The power was not locked up. It was given something to be.

When the city was abandoned the shape fell apart, and the power went back to what it had been before, shapeless and aimless, changing everything it touched into the purest form of itself.

For the first time you understand the curse completely. And you understand why the ritual needs two people.
text.ranger:
The chamber smells of nothing you have ever smelt. It is not a bad smell or a good one. It is the smell of something very old that has been at work without stopping, and has never had a chance to smell of anything, because it has never been anything but what it is.

You watch the mechanism as you would watch anything that might be dangerous, from a respectful distance, studying how it behaves and looking for whatever might tell you when it is safe to go nearer.

It breathes, after a fashion. There is a slow pulse to it, as though it were doing something very like breathing.
text.cipher:
You take the chamber as a place built for a purpose. The mechanism did the work, the break is what stopped the work, and the walls set down what the work was meant to be.

You have all that in a minute or two.

What you cannot read from anything here is who broke the mechanism, and why, and what they thought would happen when they did.

choices.text: Study the ritual on the walls, so you know what you're agreeing to.

bonus.label: You have listened to it before

success.text:
[missing person] takes you through the parts that matter. The text is close and difficult, but with their help you can follow the shape of it.

The ritual needs two people to do two matching things at once, at certain places in the chamber, and to be touching each other at the moment of sealing. The mechanism will answer to what the two of them want, together. The text has a phrase for it that [missing person] translates as unified wanting: two people wanting the same thing so clearly that the mechanism can take it as a single signal.

The danger is that the mechanism, in answering them, reads the two of them entirely. It reads more than what they want. It reads everything. The text says plainly that those who take part may learn things about themselves and each other that they would never have chosen to learn.

You look at the person you crossed an empty country to find. "Everything?" you say.

"Everything," they say.

success_at_cost.text:
You understand it in outline: two people, two matching actions, one clear wish between them, and touching at the end. The dangers you only half understand, which [missing person] points out is not ideal.

"We should come back to this before the ritual," they say. "You ought to understand all of it."

failure.text: You can't follow the ritual without more time and more preparation. [missing person] gives you the summary they have worked out over eight months of reading it, and that will have to do for now.

choices.text: Look at the break in the mechanism from the safe distance, and work out what did it.

bonus.label: You have listened to it before

success.text:
From three yards away you can read the break well enough.

It is old, twenty years at the least, which fits with when the seal began to fail. It was made by a very exact blow, with a tool made for just that purpose. It was not a weapon. It was an instrument, and somebody brought it here on purpose.

And at the very point where it struck, barely to be seen on the surface of the mechanism, there is the residue of a ritual. Whoever did this performed a ritual at the moment of striking. They did not simply break the mechanism. They operated on it.

It was not vandalism. It was surgery. Somebody took something out of the mechanism, and the break is the wound it left.

success_at_cost.text: The break was meant. It is old, and it was done for a reason. That much you can read. What exactly was done to the mechanism when it was struck, you can't make out from here.

failure.text: You can see that it is damage, old and deliberate. To learn any more you would have to go nearer than is wise.

choices.text: Go nearer than three yards, and listen to the thread.

success.text:
[missing person] says your name once, as a warning. You go nearer anyway.

At arm's length from the break, the thread is not silent. It is the note you felt under the inn wall, but here it is uneven, and keeps catching on something, like a song with a line cut out of the middle. Something has been taken out of the mechanism, cut out cleanly by somebody who knew where to cut.

You step back. It takes longer than it should.

success_at_cost.text: You get near enough to hear it, and it gets into you, the uneven note catching on its gap. You come back to yourself with [missing person]'s hand on your collar, pulling you away. You know now that the mechanism was cut. You don't know how long you were standing there.

failure.text: Three yards, and then two, and then nothing for a while. [missing person] gets you out. You remember the thread, and the floor, and their voice saying something over and over. You don't remember what.

choices.text: Listen to the thread from where you stand.

default.text:
You don't go any nearer. You stand at the edge of the light and let yourself hear it.

The thread is the note, and the note is wrong. It is not damaged. It has a piece missing. Somebody took a piece out of this mechanism, cleanly, as you might take a key out of a lock, and it has been trying to close round the gap ever since.

text.default:
You have been in the chamber more than an hour. [missing person] is watching you closely for the first signs that you have had too much.

"We should go," they say. "For today."

You can feel the chamber in you. It is not bad yet, nor dangerous, but it is there: a slight narrowing at the edges, and a distance between you and the things that are usually close.

default: "The ritual," you say. "Are we doing it?"

They look at you. "I should like to," they say. "But you came here for me, and I am asking you to risk yourself for Ashenveld. Those are different things. I want you to choose it, not be led into it." They pause. "We go back to the outskirts. You sleep. Tomorrow you tell me what you want to do."

default.text: Maret is where you left her in the outskirts, sitting with her back to a fallen pillar. She would not go down. She gets up as you both come out, and looks at [missing person], and says nothing.

text.commander:
"If we don't seal it," you say, "what happens?"

"Crestfall is gone in weeks," they say. "Then the next town, and the next. The mechanism is wearing faster all the time. In a year, perhaps less, the curse will have spread so far that every month will make it that much harder to stop."

It is a soldier's sort of answer. You have had to make worse decisions on less. "Tomorrow, then," you say.
text.arcane:
"And if we do the ritual and it doesn't work," you say, "what happens to us?"

They are quiet for a moment. "The text does not say much about failing. It says what is needed to succeed. It suggests that the mechanism must have a clear enough wish to answer to, and if the wish is not clear enough, it simply does not answer, and nothing happens."

They pause. "There is the other possibility, that it does answer, and the two people are not ready for what answering means. The text says less about that."
text.ranger:
You have been keeping an eye on yourself since you came into the chamber. The narrowing is mild. Time has been running a little unevenly, but not badly. You are well within what is safe.

"I can stay longer, if it's any use," you say.

"No," they say, firmly but kindly. "The first time should be short. It builds up, each time you come. You need to know how it takes you to begin with." They move towards the passage. "Tomorrow."
text.cipher:
"There are things happening in Crestfall," you say. "Seriva. Vorne. We're not the only ones with a clock running."

"I know," they say. "That is why we must be quick, and careful, and being careful means you rest today and think, before we talk about when." They pause. "I have been here fourteen months. I know how to think in this place. You have only just come. Trust me in this one thing."

choices.text: Agree. Go back to the outskirts and rest.

default.text:
You leave the chamber. The passage back seems shorter than the way in, which [missing person] tells you is usual. Time runs strangely in the chamber, and makes the hours in there feel longer. You were in there three hours, and it felt like one.

Then you are back in the outskirts, in the grey forest light, and the Watcher is at the gate as before.

You sleep in the outskirts, in a spot [missing person] has cleared and made as safe as anywhere in the ruins can be.

choices.text: "I don't need to sleep on it. I'm doing the ritual."

default.text:
They look at you.

"Not today," they say. "You need preparing, and I need to prepare you properly. But..." Their face changes. "Thank you. For not needing to think about it."

You leave the chamber and sleep in the outskirts. In the morning they will begin to teach you what you need to know.
